common_mistakes: Confusing conference call with conference room, which is a physical room for meetings.
Stressing the second word of conference, which should be the first syllable, KON.
Using conference call for a one-on-one phone call, which is simply a call.

conversation.text: We have a conference call with the New York office at nine.
The conference call had twenty people on it, and nobody talked.
Please mute when you're not speaking on the conference call.

senses.definition: To join an electrical or telephone line to a circuit or network.
senses.example: When the technician connects my house, I'll be able to access the internet.

senses.definition: To join (to another object): to attach, or to be intended to attach or capable of attaching, to another object.
senses.example: I think this piece connects to that piece over there.

senses.definition: To join: to attach, or to be intended to attach or capable of attaching, to each other.
senses.example: Both roads have the same name, but they don't connect: they're on opposite sides of the river, and there's no bridge there.

senses.definition: To arrive at an intended target; to land.
senses.example: When that roundhouse kick connected with his temple it sent him flying across the room.

senses.definition: To join (two other objects), or to join (one object) to (another object): to be a link between two objects, thereby attaching them to each other.
senses.example: The new railroad will connect the northern part of the state to the southern part.

senses.definition: To join (two other objects), or to join (one object) to (another object): to take one object and attach it to another.
senses.example: I connected the printer to the computer, but I couldn't get it work.

senses.definition: To associate; to establish a relation between.
senses.example: I didn't connect my lost jewelry with the news of an area cat burglar until the police contacted me.

senses.definition: To make a travel connection; to switch from one means of transport to another as part of the same trip.
senses.example: I'm flying to London where I connect with a flight heading to Hungary.

senses.definition: Clipping of connection. A drug dealer.
A drug dealer.
A useful friend or associate.

core.definition: To link two things or people so they are joined, or to put someone in touch by phone or online.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable. The ending -ct is a k-t cluster with no vowel after it, so don't add an 'uh' sound at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses. It is positive when describing relationships ('I really connected with her') and can be negative in slang, where a 'connect' is a drug dealer.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'connect to' for devices and networks ('connect to the Wi-Fi') and 'connect with' for people ('I connected with my coworkers'). On the phone, people say 'Can you connect me to billing?' As a noun, 'connect' informally means a useful contact, but its slang meaning of a drug dealer makes it risky in professional settings.

distinctions.note: Join stresses making two things one whole or becoming part of a group; connect stresses linking, which can happen by cable, phone or relationship without merging.
Link is often more abstract or general; connect is more concrete and common for phones, networks and people.

examples.everyday: Sorry, the signal is bad; can you connect to the Wi-Fi again?
examples.professional: I'll connect you with the data engineer who built the pipeline, so you can ask about the schema.
examples.analytical: Kant tried to connect empirical experience with the a priori forms of understanding.

nuance.analogy: A connection is like a bridge between two riverbanks; it needs something solid on both ends.
nuance.etymology: From Latin connectere, 'to tie or bind together', from con- 'together' and nectere 'to bind'.
common_mistakes: Using 'connect with' for devices or 'connect to' for people; Americans say 'connect to the network' but 'connect with a client'.
Adding an extra vowel after the final -ct, saying 'kuh-NEK-tuh' instead of 'kuh-NEKT'.

conversation.text: Please hold while I connect you.
I'm trying to connect to the meeting, but the link isn't working.
I can connect you with someone in HR.

senses.definition: To make something dangerous or toxic by introducing impurities or foreign matter.
senses.example: This water is contaminated. It isn't safe to drink.

senses.definition: To soil, stain, corrupt, or infect by contact or association.
To make unfit for use by the introduction of unwholesome or undesirable elements.
senses.example: Do not contaminate the peanut butter with the jelly.

senses.definition: To infect, usually of a deadly virus.
Contaminated.
Dirty, sinful, wicked, gross, etc.

core.definition: To make something dirty, unsafe, or unfit for use by adding harmful or unwanted substances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TAM, and the final syllable rhymes with 'eight'. The middle vowel is short and reduced, so don't pronounce every letter.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies something harmful or spoiled.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for food, water, soil, and lab samples, as in 'The meat was contaminated.' It can also be used figuratively for someone's reputation or mind, but that sense is more formal. In casual talk, 'get dirty' or 'ruin' is more common.

distinctions.note: Pollute is usually used for air, water, or the environment on a large scale, while contaminate is more common for food, samples, and specific objects.
Infect refers to germs entering a living body, while contaminate refers to making something impure.

examples.everyday: Don't let the raw chicken touch the salad, or it could contaminate everything.
examples.professional: A stray variable in the training pipeline could contaminate our evaluation results.
examples.analytical: Argument by association can contaminate our judgment of a claim by tying it to a discredited source.

nuance.analogy: Contamination is like a drop of dye falling into clean water: the whole glass changes color, even if the drop seemed small.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contaminare, to touch, defile, or pollute.
common_mistakes: Using 'contaminate' for a person who is sick; for illness, say 'infect' or 'spread'.
Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'kon-tuh-MIN-ate'.

contaminate.etymology: in Middle English; from Middle English *contaminaten* (“to defile; to infect with desease”), from *contaminat* + *-en*, from Latin *contāminātus*, the perfect passive participle of *contāminō* (“to touch together, blend, mingle, corrupt, defile”) (see…

senses.definition: The act of calling or assembling by summons.
An assembly or meeting.
An assembly of the clergy, by their representatives, to consult on ecclesiastical affairs.
An academic assembly, in which the business of a university is transacted.
A flock of eagles.

core.definition: A formal assembly of people, especially clergy or university members, called together for a ceremony or official purpose.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -KAY-, and the final -tion is pronounced 'shun.' Many learners stress the first syllable or pronounce the -tion as 'tee-on.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It names a solemn or official gathering rather than a casual one.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly for university ceremonies, such as a convocation where degrees are awarded or a new academic year begins, and for church assemblies. In everyday speech people say 'meeting,' 'assembly,' or 'ceremony' instead. It is not a casual word, so using it for a regular office meeting would sound odd.

distinctions.note: Assembly is a general word for any gathering of people, while convocation implies a formal, official summons to a ceremony or institutional event.
A synod is a formal church council of bishops or elders, while a convocation can be any formal gathering, including academic ones.

examples.everyday: My daughter's college convocation is on Saturday, so we're all driving up for the ceremony.
examples.professional: The university will hold its fall convocation in the main auditorium, and the provost will give the welcome address.
examples.analytical: The medieval convocation of clergy gathered not only to debate doctrine but also to assert the church's corporate authority over its members.

nuance.analogy: A convocation is like a formal roll call of a whole community, where people come together under a single official summons.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convocatio, 'a calling together,' from convocare, 'to call together,' from con- 'together' and vocare 'to call.'
common_mistakes: Using it for a casual meeting; it sounds overly formal in normal office talk.
Confusing it with 'convocation' as a verb, which is the verb 'convoke.'

convocation.etymology: From Middle English *convocacioun*, from Old French *convocation*, from Latin *convocatio*.

senses.definition: Imparting or improving beauty, particularly the beauty of the complexion.
senses.example: a cosmetic preparation

senses.definition: External or superficial; pertaining only to the surface or appearance of something.
senses.example: Fortunately, the damage to the house was mostly cosmetic and a bit of paint covered it nicely.

senses.definition: Any substances applied to enhance the external color or texture of the skin, e.g. lipstick, eyeshadow, eyeliner.
A feature existing only on the surface.
An intangible influence that improves the overall perception of some thing or situation.

core.definition: Improving how someone looks, especially the skin, or affecting only the surface appearance of something rather than its substance.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, 'MEH', not on the first. The final syllable is a short 'ik', so do not add an extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cosmetic for makeup and beauty products, as in 'cosmetic products', and for changes that improve appearance only, as in 'cosmetic repairs'. The noun cosmetics, usually plural, is the everyday word for makeup. When used about a problem, cosmetic can imply that the deeper issue is still there, which may sound dismissive.

distinctions.note: Superficial is a broader judgment about shallowness, while cosmetic specifically refers to appearance or surface changes that improve looks.
Aesthetic concerns the principles of beauty and taste, while cosmetic refers to the practical act of improving surface appearance.

examples.everyday: She bought some new cosmetic products at the drugstore, mostly lipstick and mascara.
examples.professional: The redesign is mostly cosmetic, so the backend code and the database schema stay exactly the same.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the reform is merely cosmetic, because it changes the appearance of the policy while leaving its underlying incentives untouched.

nuance.analogy: A cosmetic change is like repainting a house: it looks new from the street, but the wiring and foundation are still the same.
nuance.etymology: From Greek kosmetikos, meaning skilled in arranging or adorning, from kosmein, to arrange or adorn.
common_mistakes: Using cosmetic as a noun in the singular for makeup, when Americans usually say cosmetics in the plural.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'COS-metic'.

cosmetic.etymology: From French *cosmétique*, from Ancient Greek *κοσμητική* (“the art of dress and ornament”), *κοσμητικός*, from *κοσμητής* (“orderer, director, decorator”), from *κοσμέω* (“to order, to arrange, to rule, to adorn, to equip, to dress, to embellish”), from…

senses.definition: That is both countable and infinite; having the same cardinality as the set of natural numbers; formally, such that a bijection exists from ℕ to the set.

core.definition: Infinite but able to be matched one-to-one with the natural numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, forever.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on KOWN in countably and on IN in infinite. The -ably ending is pronounced 'uh-blee', not 'ay-blee', which is a common spelling trap.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise technical term used in mathematics and computer science.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists in the US use countably infinite to describe sets like the integers or the rationals. It is not used in casual speech. In a lecture or paper, you can say 'the set is countably infinite' and expect that everyone will understand it.

distinctions.note: A finite set has a fixed number of elements, while a countably infinite set never ends but can still be listed in order.
Uncountably infinite sets, such as the real numbers, are too large to be listed one by one, even in principle.

examples.everyday: My kid asked if there are more numbers than there are stars, and I said the whole number line is countably infinite, which made him laugh.
examples.professional: The dataset has countably infinite possible keys in theory, but in practice we only store a finite subset.
examples.analytical: Cantor showed that the rationals are countably infinite, while the reals are uncountably infinite, so the two infinities differ in size.

nuance.analogy: It is like an endless staircase where you can count every step by number, even though there is no top.
nuance.etymology: Countable from count plus -able, and infinite from Latin infinitus, 'unbounded'.
common_mistakes: Stressing ably as 'ay-blee'; the ending is 'uh-blee'.
Using countably infinite to mean 'very large' in everyday speech; it has a precise mathematical meaning.

senses.definition: Either of two parts that fit together or otherwise complement one another.
senses.example: Those brass knobs and their hollow counterparts interlock perfectly.

senses.definition: A duplicate of a legal document.
One who or that which resembles another. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
One who or that which has corresponding functions or characteristics.
senses.example: Her French counterpart attended the meeting via video call.

senses.definition: Either half of a flattened fossil when the rock has split along the plane of the fossil.
To counterbalance. (Can we add an example for this sense?)

core.definition: A person or thing that matches or corresponds to another in a different place, role, or system.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KOWN, with a lighter secondary stress on -pahrt. The middle syllable is a reduced American r-colored vowel, so say it as 'tur,' not 'tar.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a descriptive word with no positive or negative charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use counterpart constantly in work and social settings to mean the equivalent person in another organization or role, such as 'my counterpart at the other company.' It is neutral in tone and works in meetings, email, and casual talk alike. The sense 'one of two complementary parts' is common too, as in 'the counterpart to this lid.'

distinctions.note: Equivalent stresses equal value or function; counterpart stresses the matching role in a parallel structure, usually a person or unit.
A match is something that fits or pairs well with another; a counterpart is a parallel entity in a different context.

examples.everyday: I talked to my counterpart at the other branch, and she said their office closes early on Fridays.
examples.professional: Can you set up a call with your counterpart on the vendor side so we can sort out the invoice?
examples.analytical: Each concept in the classical account has a counterpart in the modern one, though the two differ in their underlying assumptions.

nuance.analogy: Like the other half of a pair of gloves: each one has a counterpart that matches it in a different position.
nuance.etymology: From counter- (opposite, against) and part (a portion), a part that answers to another.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'tar' rather than a reduced 'tur'.
Using 'counterpart' for an opponent; it means a matching or parallel one, not a rival.

counterpart.etymology: From Middle English *conterpart*, *countre parte* (“duplicate of a legal document”), equivalent to *counter-* + *part*.

senses.definition: To lie down for a long rest, sleep or nap, as from tiredness or exhaustion.
To collide with something destructively; to fall or come down violently.
senses.example: When the car crashed into a house, the driver was heavily injured.

senses.definition: To cause something to collide with something else, especially when this results in damage.
senses.example: I'm sorry for crashing the bike into a wall. I'll pay for repairs.

senses.definition: To hit or strike with force.
To make a sudden loud noise.
senses.example: Thunder crashed directly overhead.

senses.definition: Ellipsis of gatecrash.
senses.example: We weren't invited to the party so we decided to crash it.

senses.definition: To accelerate a project or a task or its schedule by devoting more resources to it.
To make or experience informal temporary living arrangements, especially overnight.
senses.example: Hey dude, can I crash at your pad?

senses.definition: To give, as a favor.
To experience a period of depression and/or lethargy after a period of euphoria, as after the euphoric effect of a psychotropic drug has dissipated.
To terminate or halt execution due to an exception.
senses.example: If the system crashes again, we'll have it fixed in the computer shop.

senses.definition: To cause an exception that terminates or halts execution.
senses.example: Double-clicking this icon crashes the desktop.

senses.definition: To take a sudden and severe turn for the worse; to rapidly and catastrophically deteriorate.
An automobile, airplane, or other vehicle accident.
senses.example: She broke two bones in her body in a car crash.

senses.definition: A malfunction of computer software or hardware which causes it to shut down or become partially or totally inoperable.
senses.example: My computer had a crash so I had to reboot it.

senses.definition: A sudden, intense, loud sound, as made for example by cymbals.
senses.example: The piece ended in a crescendo, building up to a crash of cymbals.

senses.definition: A sudden large decline in the value of money, stocks or other assets, etc. especially one that causes additional economic difficulties.
senses.example: the stock market crash

senses.definition: A comedown from a drug.
A group of rhinoceroses.
A sudden decline in any living form's population levels, often leading to extinction.
Tarlatan, mull.
A type of rough linen.
Quick, fast, intensive, impromptu.
senses.example: crash course

core.definition: To collide violently with something, such as a car hitting another car, a wall, or the ground.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and say a clear 'r' at the start. The 'sh' is a hard, short sound, and the vowel is the short 'a' of 'cat'.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing accidents or failures; neutral or friendly when used for sleeping over at someone's home.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use crash for car accidents, for a computer or app that stops working, and in casual speech for sleeping at someone's place. To say you will sleep over, say 'Can I crash at your place tonight?' A common reply is 'Sure, you can crash on the couch.' For a serious car accident, Americans say 'car accident' or 'wreck' rather than always 'crash'.

distinctions.note: Collide is more formal and suggests two moving objects hitting each other; crash is more casual and often implies a loud, damaging impact.
Wreck is a strong everyday word for a serious accident or ruined state; crash is more general and can also describe software failure.

examples.everyday: Can I crash at your place tonight? I missed the last train.
examples.professional: The build failed because the app crashed every time someone opened the settings page.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that a single collision can crash an entire system when every part depends on the others.

nuance.analogy: Crashing is like a dropped glass: one sudden impact breaks what was working smoothly.
nuance.etymology: Probably imitative of a loud breaking or smashing sound, appearing in English in the 1600s.
common_mistakes: Using 'crash' for a slight bump; it implies a strong, damaging impact.
Saying 'I will crash your home' instead of 'crash at your place', which is the natural idiom.

crash.etymology: From Middle English *crasshen*, *crasschen*, *craschen* (“to break into pieces”), of uncertain origin.

conversation.text: He walked away from the crash with just a few bruises.
She crashed into a pole on the icy road.
My laptop crashed in the middle of my presentation.
Can I crash at your place tonight? My flight got canceled.
You can crash on our couch if it gets too late.
I got home and crashed right away.
Some guys we didn't know crashed the party.
He crashed his car on the highway, but he's okay.

senses.definition: Characteristic of or suitable to a creature, often specifically a non-human animal.

core.definition: Relating to or belonging to created beings, especially in their dependence on God and their physical limits.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make 'ture' sound like 'chur'. The final 'ly' is a light 'lee' sound, not a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to somewhat solemn; it emphasizes human limits and dependence and can sound poetic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use creaturely mostly in theology, philosophy, and literary writing about the physical or dependent nature of living beings. It may describe animals, especially in discussions of nature, or humans who depend on God. In casual conversation, people usually say 'animal' or 'human' instead. A natural reply in a discussion is 'Yes, that captures our limits well.'

distinctions.note: Creaturely means of or belonging to created beings, while creative means inventive or imaginative.
Animal describes a specific kind of living thing, while creaturely can describe any created being in a theological sense.

examples.everyday: After hiking all day, I felt very creaturely, hungry and tired and ready for a nap.
examples.professional: Our product design should account for creaturely needs such as rest, attention, and fatigue.
examples.analytical: Bonhoeffer's account of human life stresses its creaturely limits, which point us toward dependence on God.

nuance.analogy: Creaturely is like a candle flame: real and bright, but it depends on a source beyond itself.
nuance.etymology: From creature plus -ly, forming an adjective meaning like or suited to a creature.
common_mistakes: Using creaturely to mean creative; the two words are unrelated in meaning.
Assuming it only describes animals; in theology it refers to all created beings, including humans.

senses.definition: A soft mass of material stuffed into a cloth bag, used for comfort or support. A throw pillow.
A thin, flat pad used on hard chairs and sometimes toilet seats.
Something acting as a cushion, especially to absorb a shock or impact.
A pad on which gilders cut gold leaf.
A mass of steam in the end of the cylinder of a steam engine to receive the impact of the piston.
The pillow used in making bone lace.
An engraver's pad.

A sufficient quantity of an intangible object (like points or minutes) to allow for some of those points, for example, to be lost without hurting one's chances for successfully completing an objective.
Money kept in reserve.
The lip around a table in cue sports which absorbs some of the impact of the billiard balls and bounces them back.
(historical) The rubber of an electrical machine.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) A pad supporting a woman's hair.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (historical) The dancer in the cushion dance who currently holds the cushion, or the dance itself.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: To furnish with cushions.
senses.example: to cushion a sofa

senses.definition: To seat or place on, or as on a cushion.
To absorb or deaden the impact of.
senses.example: to cushion a blow

senses.definition: To conceal or cover up, as under a cushion.

core.definition: A soft pad, often filled with foam or stuffing, used for comfort when sitting or kneeling, or for support.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final -ion is a weak un sound, not ee-on. The sh is clear, and the t is absent, so do not say the word with a t sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. A cushion suggests comfort, softness, and protection.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cushion for a pillow on a chair or sofa, and also for a seat pad. A throw pillow is a decorative pillow on a couch, while a cushion is often attached to a chair or used for sitting. In everyday speech people often just say pillow for a soft item on a couch.

distinctions.note: A pillow is usually for sleeping, while a cushion is usually for sitting, kneeling, or decoration on furniture.
A pad is a thinner, flatter layer, often used for protection, while a cushion is softer and thicker for comfort.

examples.everyday: Can you grab a cushion for the wooden chair? My back is sore.
examples.professional: We should add a cushion to the budget in case the vendor delays the delivery.
examples.analytical: The text uses the image of a cushion to suggest how grace softens the blow of judgment.

nuance.analogy: A cushion is like a soft layer between your body and a hard surface, absorbing pressure so you feel less of it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French coissin, from Late Latin coxinum, a cushion or pillow.
common_mistakes: Saying cushion for a bed pillow, when Americans usually say pillow for sleeping
Using cushion as a verb without a preposition, when the usual pattern is cushion something against or from a blow

cushion.etymology: From Middle English *quysshyn*, from later Old French *coissin* (modern *coussin*), from Vulgar Latin **coxīnus* (“seat pad”), derived from Latin *coxa* (“hip, thigh”) (with the suffix possibly after *pulvīnus* (“pillow”)), ultimately from…

senses.definition: To cut upward.
To cut into smaller pieces, parts, or sections.
senses.example: With a little practice, you can cut up a whole chicken yourself for frying.

senses.definition: To lacerate; to wound by multiple lacerations; to injure or damage by cutting, or as if by cutting.
senses.example: The attackers cut him up pretty bad.

senses.definition: To distress mentally or emotionally.
To behave like a clown or jokester (a cut-up); to misbehave; to act in a playful, comical, boisterous, or unruly manner to elicit laughter, attention, etc.
senses.example: We need to talk about Johnny's tendency to cut up in class.

senses.definition: To disintegrate; to break into pieces.
Comprise a particular selection of runners.
senses.example: The race has cut up badly with no real opposition to "Serendipity".

senses.definition: (dated) To severely criticize or censure; to subject to hostile criticism.
senses.example: The reviewer cut up the book mercilessly.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: (dated) To divide into portions well or badly; to have the property left at one's death turn out well or poorly when divided among heirs, legatees, etc.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Having been cut into smaller pieces.
senses.example: Put the cut up vegetables in the pot.

senses.definition: Wounded with multiple lacerations.
senses.example: He is cut up pretty bad.

senses.definition: Muscular and lean.
senses.example: I go to the gym to get stronger and cut up.

core.definition: To cut food into smaller pieces, such as chopping vegetables or meat, usually before cooking or serving.

pronunciation.tip: 'Up' is the stressed word, so say 'kut-UP'. The 'u' in 'up' is the short 'uh' vowel, not the long 'oo' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing ordinary food preparation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'cut up' for food in the kitchen, such as 'cut up the chicken' or 'cut up the fruit for the kids'. It is casual and common at home. For the adjective 'cut up' describing a person, it also means wounded or physically hurt, so be careful with that sense.

distinctions.note: 'Chop' means cutting with a knife into rough pieces, while 'cut up' is more general and can mean cutting into any sized pieces.
'Dice' means to cut into small, even cubes, while 'cut up' does not require uniform size.

examples.everyday: Can you cut up the apples for the kids while I start the pasta?
examples.professional: The kitchen team cuts up the vegetables before the dinner rush so service stays fast.
examples.analytical: Cutting up a whole text into quotations can make an argument look more fragmented than the original.

nuance.analogy: Like breaking a candy bar into bite-sized pieces so everyone gets a share.
nuance.etymology: 'Cut' (to divide with a blade) plus the adverb 'up' (into pieces).
common_mistakes: Using 'cut up' as a noun in a sentence where 'cutting' or 'pieces' is needed, such as 'I did a cut up of the onions'.
Forgetting that 'cut up' for a person means wounded or hurt, which is a different sense from kitchen use.

conversation.text: Can you cut up the chicken for the baby?
I cut up some apples for a snack.
Cut up the potatoes into small pieces.

core.definition: The name of several Persian kings in the Bible, most notably Darius I, who allowed the rebuilding of the Temple in Jerusalem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, and the middle vowel is a reduced schwa. Many learners stress the first syllable, but in American speech the stress is on the 'rye' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, used in historical or biblical contexts; it is also a common given name.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'Darius' as a name and for the Persian kings. In Bible study, 'Darius' can refer to Darius I, Darius the Mede in Daniel, or Darius II in Nehemiah. Context usually shows which one is meant.

distinctions.vs: Darius the Mede vs. Darius I
distinctions.note: 'Darius the Mede' is a figure in Daniel whose historical identity is debated, while Darius I was a historical Persian king.

examples.everyday: My friend named his son Darius, and everyone calls him Dare for short.
examples.professional: In the historical timeline slide, I placed Darius I after Cyrus and before Xerxes.
examples.analytical: The decree of Darius in Ezra 6 presents the Persian king as a patron of the Jerusalem Temple, which shaped post-exilic theology.

nuance.analogy: Darius is like a family name that appears in several generations, and you must check the context to know which one is meant.
nuance.etymology: From Old Persian 'Darayavaush', meaning 'holding firm the good' or similar.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable instead of the second.
Assuming all Dariuses in the Bible are the same king.
nuance.biblical_note: Darius appears in several Bible books as a Persian king, mainly in Ezra, Nehemiah, Daniel and Haggai. Hebrew: Daryavesh, from Old Persian. Ezra 6:1-12 describes Darius I's decree that allowed the Temple rebuilding and ordered support for it. Daniel 5:31 introduces Darius the Mede, who receives the kingdom after Belshazzar. Haggai 1:1 dates the prophecy to the second year of Darius.

senses.definition: An individual act of debauchery.
An orgy.
To morally corrupt (someone); to seduce.
To debase (something); to lower the value of (something).
To indulge in revelry.

core.definition: An episode of excessive, immoral indulgence in pleasure, such as drinking, sex, or gambling. Often used in literary or formal writing.

pronunciation.tip: As a noun, stress the first syllable, DEB. The verb is stressed on the second syllable, dih-BAWCH, so the noun and verb differ in stress. The ending rhymes with 'lawsuit' and 'coach' sounds mostly like 'awch' in General American.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes morally troubling excess and carries a strong sense of disapproval.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet debauch in books, sermons, news about scandals, or formal criticism rather than daily talk. Saying it in casual conversation can sound dramatic or old-fashioned. For everyday speech, people say 'a wild night' or 'a party that got out of hand'.

distinctions.note: Debauch is a single act or episode; debauchery is the general condition or practice of excess.
An orgy refers specifically to sexual excess in a group; debauch covers a wider range of moral excess.

examples.everyday: After the wedding, the groomsmen went on a debauch that nobody talks about anymore.
examples.professional: The consultant's report described the company's spending spree as a financial debauch that the board had ignored.
examples.analytical: For the author, the aristocrat's debauch exposes the moral emptiness that lies beneath his wealth.

nuance.analogy: A debauch is like a sudden flood of excess that washes away good judgment for a time.
nuance.etymology: From Old French debauchier, meaning to entice from duty or to lead astray.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun's stress (DEB-awch) with the verb's stress (dih-BAWCH).
Using debauch casually for ordinary parties, which sounds much too strong in everyday speech.

debauch.etymology: 1590s, from Middle French *desbaucher* (“entice from work or duty”), from Old French *desbauchier* (“to lead astray”), from *des-* + *bauch* (“beam”), from **balkō*, from Proto-Germanic **balkô*, from Proto-Indo-European **bʰelǵ-* (“beam, plank”); latter…

senses.definition: Laughable, ridiculous, especially due to being small, inadequate, or low-quality; provoking derision.
Expressing derision; mocking; ridiculing.

core.definition: So small, inadequate or low that it seems laughable, such as a derisory offer; also mocking in tone.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RY. The -ory ending is usually reduced to ree in American speech, with the r pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Negative: it suggests that something is too small or poor to be taken seriously.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use derisory mainly in formal writing or news, often describing offers, pay, or amounts, such as a derisory salary. It is used more often in British English, so many Americans would say ridiculously low or laughably small instead. Using it casually can sound stiff.

distinctions.note: Derisive describes a mocking attitude; derisory describes something so inadequate that it deserves mockery.
Insufficient is neutral and factual; derisory adds a judgment that the amount is laughably poor.

examples.everyday: The landlord offered a derisory increase, so I didn't even bother to respond.
examples.professional: The vendor's derisory bid was far below our budget, so we rejected it without a counteroffer.
examples.analytical: The report calls the government's derisory funding for research a failure of political imagination.

nuance.analogy: Like offering a single coin to pay for a meal: the gesture is so small it becomes a joke.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin derisorius, from Latin deridere, to mock.
common_mistakes: Using derisory to mean derisive, as in a derisory laugh; derisory describes something small or poor.
Pronouncing it as DEH-ri-sor-ee with a heavy r and long vowels.

senses.definition: To cease to proceed or act; to stop.
senses.example: Please desist from telephoning me at this number.

core.definition: To stop doing something, especially something unwanted or annoying; to cease. Usually followed by 'from' plus a gerund.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the initial s is voiceless, as in 'sit'. Learners often stress the first syllable or voice the s like a z.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to firm. It signals an authority or a clear order to stop, so it can sound stern when used to a person.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'desist' mostly in formal notices, legal letters, and official instructions, such as 'Desist from further violations.' In everyday talk they say 'stop,' 'quit,' or 'knock it off.' Saying 'Please desist' to a roommate would sound stiff or mocking. A natural reply is simply to stop the behavior or to say 'Okay, I'll stop.'

distinctions.note: 'Stop' is everyday and neutral; 'desist' is formal and often used for stopping a behavior that someone has been told to end.
'Cease' suggests bringing something to a complete end, often over time, and is common in formal and legal writing; 'desist' focuses on stopping an action in response to a demand.
'Quit' is informal and can mean stopping a habit or job; 'desist' is more formal and is nearly always about a behavior.

examples.everyday: My neighbor asked the kids to desist from kicking the ball against his fence.
examples.professional: Legal has asked the vendor to desist from using our trademark in future marketing materials.
examples.analytical: The author argues that the state should desist from interfering with private religious practice.

nuance.analogy: Desist is like pressing the brake on an action and bringing it to a complete stop because someone with authority told you to.
nuance.etymology: From Latin desistere, 'to stand off or leave off,' from de- 'away' and sistere 'to stand.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'desist to do' instead of 'desist from doing.'
Stressing the first syllable (DIS-ist) instead of the second.
Using 'desist' in casual speech, where it sounds unnatural.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a despot or tyrant.
senses.example: This despotic age of the empire ended in a revolt.

senses.definition: Acting or ruling as a despot, tyrannical.
senses.example: The despotic king dissolved the parliament, and took personal control of the country.

core.definition: Ruling with absolute, unchecked power, often in a harsh or oppressive way.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, PAH, with the American open 'ah' vowel. The final -ic is a short 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes harsh, controlling authority that ignores the rights of others.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use despotic in political analysis, history and literary writing about rulers or institutions. In everyday talk they would more often say bossy, controlling or tyrannical. Describing a manager as despotic is possible but sounds deliberate and serious.

distinctions.note: Tyrannical is more common in everyday English; despotic is more formal and stresses absolute, personal rule.
Autocratic describes a neutral system of one-person rule; despotic adds a clear sense of cruelty.
Authoritarian is broader and often used in political science; despotic is more personal and harsh.

examples.everyday: My sister says her new landlord is despotic about the rules, so nobody dares to ask for repairs.
examples.professional: Some software teams run under despotic leads who approve every decision and ignore input from engineers.
examples.analytical: Montesquieu argues that despotic government rests on fear, while monarchy depends on honor and law.

nuance.analogy: A despotic ruler is like a thermostat with no limits: it controls everything in the room and lets no one adjust it.
nuance.etymology: From despot, from Greek despotes, 'master, lord'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'des-POT-ic' with the stress on the wrong syllable; the stress is on PAH.
Using despotic as a casual word for strict, which overstates the cruelty in American speech.

despotic.etymology: From Ancient Greek *δεσποτικός* via French *despotique*, equivalent to *despot* + *-ic*.

senses.definition: To use one’s intellect to plan or design (something).
senses.example: to devise an argument; to devise a machine, or a new system of writing

senses.definition: To leave (property) in a will.
The act of leaving real property in a will.
Such a will, or a clause in such a will.
The real property left in such a will.
Design, devising.

core.definition: To invent or plan something carefully, such as a method, system, or scheme; also, to leave real property by will.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable. The final sound is a 'z', so it rhymes with 'rise' and not 'dice'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it suggests thoughtful creation of a plan or solution.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use devise in workplace and formal settings to mean come up with a plan or method, such as devise a strategy. In casual speech, people more often say come up with or think up. In legal English, the verb and noun refer to leaving real property in a will.

distinctions.note: Invent suggests creating something new; devise stresses planning or designing a method for a purpose.
Design usually refers to shape, structure, or appearance; devise is about the plan or method behind it.

examples.everyday: We need to devise a way to get the couch up the stairs.
examples.professional: Our team will devise a rollback plan before we deploy the new model.
examples.analytical: Aquinas argues that human reason can devise laws, but these laws must be ordered toward the common good.

nuance.analogy: To devise a plan is like drawing a map before a road trip, deciding the route before the car starts.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'deviser', from Latin 'divisare', meaning to divide or arrange, from 'dividere'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it like 'device' (DIH-vice); the verb ends in a z sound.
Using devise for simply finding or making something without planning.
patterns: devise a way to do sth

devise.etymology: From Middle English *devisen*, *devysen*, from Old French *deviser*, from Vulgar Latin *devisō*, from Latin *dīvisō*, frequentative of *dīvidō*.

senses.definition: Transparent or translucent; allowing light to pass through; capable of being seen through.
Of a fine, almost transparent, texture; gossamer; light and insubstantial.
Isorefractive, having an identical refractive index.

core.definition: Very thin and light, so that it is almost transparent and lets light or shapes pass through, like a delicate fabric.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AF, the second syllable. The first syllable is 'dye', and the unstressed syllables reduce to 'uh' and 'us'. Do not stress the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Positive and descriptive; it suggests delicacy, beauty, or a dreamy quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use diaphanous mostly in fashion writing, poetry, and descriptive prose about fabric, light, or mist. It sounds poetic in everyday speech, so people usually say 'sheer' or 'see-through' in casual talk. Use it when you want an elegant or literary image.

distinctions.note: Sheer is the common everyday word for thin fabric; diaphanous is more literary and emphasizes an airy, ethereal quality.
Translucent means letting light through but blurring shapes; diaphanous often implies a fine, light texture that is still delicate and graceful.

examples.everyday: She wore a diaphanous white scarf that floated in the wind at the wedding.
examples.professional: The designer chose a diaphanous silk for the spring collection, which photographs beautifully under studio lights.
examples.analytical: Keats uses diaphanous imagery to suggest a world that is delicate, passing, and difficult to grasp.

nuance.analogy: Diaphanous fabric is like morning mist: you can see through it, but it softens everything behind it.
nuance.etymology: From Greek diaphanēs, 'transparent,' from dia- 'through' and phainein 'to show.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable as 'DYE-uh-fan-us'.
Using diaphanous for opaque or heavy fabric, which is the opposite meaning.

diaphanous.etymology: From Medieval Latin *diaphanus*, from Ancient Greek *διαφανής*, from *δια-* (“through”) + *φαίνω* (“to shine, appear”).

senses.definition: Reminding someone to protect their skin from the sun.

core.definition: A question asking whether someone applied sunscreen to protect their skin from the sun before going outside.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SCREEN in 'sunscreen', and the first syllable is reduced to 'suhn'. In 'put on', the particle 'on' takes some stress, and the words link together quickly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to caring. It can sound helpful, but it can also sound like a reminder that someone might find slightly nagging.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this before outdoor trips, at the beach, or to children before school recess. Among adults it can sound like a gentle reminder, so it works best with family or close friends. A natural reply is 'Yep, already did!' or 'Oops, let me put some on now.'

distinctions.note: 'Sunblock' is an older or more emphatic term for products with stronger protection; Americans use sunscreen for most products.
This asks about the result, while 'Did you put on sunscreen?' asks about the preventive action.

examples.everyday: Did you put on sunscreen before we left? It is going to be strong at the beach today.
examples.professional: Did you put on sunscreen before the outdoor offsite? We will be in the sun for hours.
examples.analytical: The clinician's first question was whether the patient had put on sunscreen before the long hike.

nuance.analogy: It works like a raincoat for your skin: you put it on before the weather hits.
common_mistakes: Saying 'put sunscreen' without 'on' in casual speech; Americans say 'put on sunscreen' or 'wear sunscreen'.
Pronouncing 'sunscreen' with the stress on SUN; the stress is on SCREEN.

conversation.text: Did you put on sunscreen? It's really sunny today.
Did you put on sunscreen, or do I need to do it?
Did you put on sunscreen? Your nose is getting pink.

senses.definition: Possessing mental discipline.
Under control.
Relating to a specified kind or number of disciplines.

core.definition: Showing self-control, regular habits and the ability to follow rules or a plan, especially when work is hard.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, DIS. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so it sounds like 'DIS-uh-plund', and the final 'ed' is a soft 'd' sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises self-control, focus and reliable habits.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disciplined' to praise someone who sticks to a routine, such as 'She's very disciplined about exercise.' It is common in everyday talk, in job descriptions and in sports. It can also describe an organized group, such as 'a disciplined army' or 'a disciplined team'.

distinctions.note: 'Strict' describes rules set by someone else, while 'disciplined' describes self-control that a person practices..
'Organized' describes how things are arranged, while 'disciplined' describes the behavior of people who follow a plan.

examples.everyday: My brother is very disciplined about his workouts, so he goes to the gym every morning.
examples.professional: The team has a disciplined review process, so every change is tested before release.
examples.analytical: A disciplined mind does not follow every impulse, but weighs evidence before forming a judgment.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-trained runner who keeps to the training plan even on days when they feel tired.
nuance.etymology: From 'discipline' (Latin disciplina, teaching or instruction) plus the adjective ending '-ed'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'disciplined' with three full syllables; the middle vowel is weak.
Confusing it with 'disciplinary', which means relating to punishment or discipline procedures.

senses.definition: The act of revealing something.
The making known of a previously hidden fact or series of facts to another party; the act of disclosing.
senses.example: get full disclosure

senses.definition: That which is disclosed; a previously hidden fact or series of facts that is made known.

core.definition: The act of making known a previously hidden fact, or the fact itself that has been made known.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, kloh. The middle sound is the 'zh' sound as in 'measure,' and the final syllable is a reduced, rhotic r sound, so don't say it as 'dis-KLOH-zher.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to serious. In legal or corporate contexts it can carry weight, and a sudden disclosure can sound alarming.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use disclosure in business, law, medicine, and finance, and also in news reporting, as in 'a disclosure of documents.' In everyday talk they usually say 'coming out' or 'telling someone' for personal matters. Disclosure is common in phrases like 'full disclosure,' which means telling all the relevant facts.

distinctions.note: A revelation is a surprising discovery that changes understanding, while a disclosure is a formal or deliberate act of sharing information.
A confession is an admission of one's own guilt or wrongdoing, whereas disclosure can refer to any information shared.
An announcement is a public declaration, usually of good or neutral news, while a disclosure often reveals something that was previously hidden.

examples.everyday: The sudden disclosure that my neighbor had moved away surprised everyone on the street.
examples.professional: The compliance team reviewed the disclosure requirements before the quarterly report went out.
examples.analytical: Heidegger's notion of disclosure, or aletheia, suggests that truth is not simply a matter of correct statements but of things becoming visible.

nuance.analogy: A disclosure is like turning on a light in a closed room, suddenly showing what was there all along.
nuance.etymology: From disclose plus the suffix -ure, forming a noun of action or result.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle sound as 'k-s' rather than the soft 'zh' sound.
Using disclosure to mean a single small comment; it usually refers to a more significant revealing of facts.

senses.definition: The condition of being out of favor; loss of favor, regard, or respect.
The state of being dishonored, or covered with shame.
senses.example: Now she lives in disgrace.

senses.definition: Someone or something which brings dishonor; the cause of reproach or shame; great discredit.
senses.example: His behavior at the party was a total disgrace! He was leeching on all the ladies, and insulting the men.

senses.definition: To put someone or something out of favor; to bring shame or ignominy upon.

core.definition: A loss of respect or honor, or a person or thing that brings shame, embarrassment, or strong criticism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, -GRAYS. The 'r' is clear in American speech, and the final 's' is a true 's' sound, not 'z'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes shame or loss of respect, often strongly.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disgrace' in both everyday and formal speech, for example 'That referee is a disgrace.' In casual talk, it can be a strong insult, so use it with care. In formal writing, 'disgrace' often describes a public loss of honor, such as a scandal or dismissal.

distinctions.note: Shame is a personal feeling of guilt or embarrassment; disgrace is a public loss of respect or honor.
Embarrassment is usually mild and temporary; disgrace is much more serious and lasting.

examples.everyday: That parking lot is a disgrace, with potholes everywhere.
examples.professional: The unresolved outage was a disgrace for a team that prides itself on reliability.
examples.analytical: Socrates was condemned not for corrupting the youth alone but for the disgrace his trial brought upon the city.

nuance.analogy: Disgrace is like losing a badge of honor: you still have the item, but it no longer shows that you are respected.
nuance.etymology: From Italian disgrazia (misfortune), from dis- plus grazia (grace, favor).
common_mistakes: Using 'disgrace' as a verb with the wrong preposition; say 'disgrace yourself' or 'disgrace the family,' not 'disgrace of.'
Confusing it with 'disgraceful' in conversation; 'That is a disgrace' is the noun form, while 'That is disgraceful' is the adjective.

senses.definition: That can be disposed of.
That is designed to be discarded rather than reused, refilled or repaired.
senses.example: Rather than purchase an expensive razor he bought a packet of cheap disposable ones.

senses.definition: Available to be used; at one's disposal.
senses.example: disposable income

senses.definition: Any object that is designed to be disposed of, rather than refilled or repaired.
A disposable vaporizer, as for nicotine or a concentrate of cannabis (THC).

core.definition: Designed to be thrown away after one use, rather than cleaned, refilled, or repaired.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'POH', the second syllable. The final syllable is a syllabic 'l' with no vowel, so it sounds like 'bul'. Avoid pronouncing the 's' as a 'z' in the first syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it suggests convenience and low cost, though sometimes it implies something cheap or wasteful, especially in environmental discussions.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'disposable' constantly for things like cups, razors, gloves, and diapers. When talking about environmental impact, people may describe items as 'single-use' instead. The noun form is less common in speech, where people say 'disposables' for a category of such items.

distinctions.note: 'Single-use' is preferred in environmental and medical contexts to stress that an item is used once; 'disposable' is the everyday term.
'Throwaway' is informal and often negative, suggesting something cheap or wasteful; 'disposable' is more neutral.

examples.everyday: Can you grab some disposable plates for the picnic?
examples.professional: We switched to disposable test cartridges to reduce the lab's cleaning costs.
examples.analytical: The critique treats modern consumer goods as disposable, revealing how design encourages waste.

nuance.analogy: A disposable item is like a paper napkin: you use it once and then throw it away.
nuance.etymology: From 'dispose' plus the suffix '-able,' meaning 'able to be disposed of.'
common_mistakes: Confusing 'disposable income' with 'available money' in a casual sense; the phrase is a fixed economic term.
Pronouncing the stress on the first syllable.

senses.definition: In a dogmatic manner.

core.definition: In a way that states things as absolutely certain, without openness to evidence or other views.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on MAT, and the final syllable -ly is a reduced 'lee' with a light vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it describes certainty that refuses discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use dogmatically to criticize speakers who insist on a point without support. It appears in academic reviews, debates and political commentary. In casual speech, 'stubbornly' or 'refusing to budge' is more common.

distinctions.note: 'Stubbornly' is everyday and describes refusing to change; 'dogmatically' focuses on asserting beliefs as beyond question.
'Emphatically' means forcefully, but not necessarily without evidence.

examples.everyday: He kept insisting dogmatically that the restaurant was closed, even when we could see the lights on.
examples.professional: The manager asserted dogmatically that the launch date could not move, without reviewing the risks.
examples.analytical: The critic rejects the evidence dogmatically, treating the conclusion as settled before any argument is offered.

nuance.analogy: Like a judge who hands down a verdict before hearing the witnesses.
nuance.etymology: From dogmatic, from Greek dogmatikos, from dogma.
common_mistakes: Using dogmatically as a positive word for confident speech.
Stressing the first syllable instead of MAT.

senses.definition: A bell, buzzer, or chime device mounted on or adjacent to a door's exterior, meant to be rung by a visitor to announce one's presence.
To ring many doorbells in an effort to contact people and thereby spread information or solicit.
To ring many doorbells of (target people or an area) in an effort to contact people and thereby spread information or solicit.
senses.example: We doorbelled the whole district in an effort to get out the vote.

core.definition: A button or device beside a front door that makes a ringing sound when pressed to alert people inside to a visitor.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on DOR, with the r pronounced clearly. The second syllable is a short e, rhyming with 'bell', not 'bail'. Do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a common household item.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'doorbell' for the device, and 'ring the doorbell' for visiting. Many modern homes have video doorbells. Saying 'ring the bell' alone can sound like you mean a different bell. To announce that someone is at the door, a person may say 'Someone's at the door' or 'The doorbell just rang'.

distinctions.note: A knocker is a metal fixture you strike against the door; a doorbell is an electric or mechanical device you press.
A buzzer makes a harsh noise and is common in apartment buildings to let a visitor in; a doorbell usually rings in the house.

examples.everyday: Can you get the doorbell? I think the pizza is here.
examples.professional: The smart doorbell sends a notification to the field technician when he arrives for the installation.
examples.analytical: The doorbell marks the moment a private household admits the outside world, a small threshold ritual of ordinary life.

nuance.analogy: A doorbell is like a small alarm bell at the edge of your home, announcing that someone outside is waiting to come in.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'door' (Old English 'duru') and 'bell' (Old English 'belle').
common_mistakes: Saying 'bell of the door' instead of 'doorbell'.
Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bail' instead of 'bell'.

conversation.text: The doorbell rang, but nobody was there.
Our doorbell has a camera, so I can see who's at the door.
The baby's asleep, so please knock instead of ringing the doorbell.

senses.definition: A period of unusually low rainfall, longer and more severe than a dry spell.
senses.example: His village had faced a drought twice.

senses.definition: A longer than expected term without success, particularly in sport.
senses.example: Sri Lanka ended their ten-game drought with a consolation win over Bangladesh.

core.definition: A long period with much less rain than normal, causing dry land, dying crops, and water shortages.

pronunciation.tip: The stressed vowel is the "ow" of "out," not the "ah" of "hot." The final t is a clear t, and it is not dropped as in some casual speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it signals hardship, loss, and danger, especially for farmers and communities.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use drought for a serious shortage of rain, often in news about farming, the West, or water restrictions. For a short dry period, they say dry spell. In figurative sports talk, Americans use drought for a long stretch without wins or titles, such as "a playoff drought."

distinctions.note: A dry spell is a short, informal period without rain, while a drought is a longer and more serious shortage.
Drought is a lack of water, while famine is widespread extreme hunger that often follows drought and crop failure.

examples.everyday: We have not had a good rain in three months, and this drought is hurting everyone's lawns.
examples.professional: The utility sent a notice asking customers to cut water use because of the drought.
examples.analytical: The prophet Haggai reads the drought as a sign that the people have neglected the house of the LORD.

nuance.analogy: A drought is like a bank account that keeps getting withdrawals and no deposits until nothing is left.
nuance.etymology: From Old English drūgath, dryness, from drūg, dry.
common_mistakes: Saying "dry drought" or "drought weather" when drought alone is enough.
Using drought for a single hot day; it needs a long period of little rain.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture drought is a sign of divine judgment for disobedience or a means of calling the people back to God. The Hebrew word ḥōreb means dryness or drought; the word is used in the sense of drought, as in Haggai 1:11, where the land suffers drought because the house of God lies in ruin. In 1 Kings 17:1 the prophet Elijah announces a drought that will last until he speaks again, showing that God controls the rain. In Jeremiah 17:8 the righteous person is compared to a tree that is not anxious in the year of drought, because its roots reach water.

drought.etymology: From Middle English *droughte*, *droghte*, *drouȝte*, from Old English *drūgaþ*.

senses.definition: To amuse (someone); to engage the attention of agreeably.
senses.example: to entertain friends with lively conversation

senses.definition: To have someone over at one's home, or some other venue, for a party or visit.
senses.example: They enjoy entertaining a lot.

senses.definition: To receive and take into consideration; to have a thought in mind.
senses.example: The committee would like to entertain the idea of reducing the budget figures.

core.definition: To amuse or hold someone's attention in a pleasant way, or to host guests at your home or another venue.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, TAIN. The middle -ter is a light, reduced American r-colored vowel, and the t is a flap in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests kindness and pleasant hospitality, though to entertain an idea or offer means to consider it seriously, which is neutral.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say we like to entertain when they mean hosting dinner parties or having friends over, and they often use it to describe a host's skill. When used of children or guests, it means keeping them amused. In a formal setting, an offer might be entertained, meaning considered seriously, but in everyday talk people say think about it.

distinctions.note: Amuse focuses on making someone laugh or smile, while entertain can also mean hosting people or holding their attention for longer.
Host focuses on being the person who welcomes guests and organizes an event, while entertain focuses on what happens during the visit.
Consider means to think carefully about something, and it is more neutral than entertain, which in formal use suggests you are open to an idea.

examples.everyday: We love to entertain on weekends, so our backyard is usually full of friends and their kids.
examples.professional: Our sales team will entertain clients at the conference dinner, so please keep Thursday evening free.
examples.analytical: Descartes asks whether we should entertain the possibility that our senses deceive us, and he argues that we must examine it carefully.

nuance.analogy: To entertain is like keeping a pot of coffee warm on the stove, always ready and welcoming for whoever comes through the door.
nuance.etymology: From French entretenir, from entre- (among, between) and tenir (to hold), meaning to hold among or keep up.
common_mistakes: Using entertain with a direct object meaning to have fun, as in I entertained very much at the party, when the correct form is I enjoyed myself.
Saying entertain me in the sense of please entertain my question, which sounds strange; use consider instead.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Greek philoxenia (love of strangers) is the root of hospitality, and the idea of entertaining guests appears when people welcome visitors who turn out to be messengers from God. Hebrews 13:2 urges believers to show hospitality to strangers, reminding them that some people have unknowingly welcomed angels. Genesis 18:1-8 describes Abraham hosting three visitors by the oaks of Mamre with generous food and care. Romans 12:13 calls Christians to practice hospitality as part of sharing with fellow believers in need.

entertain.etymology: From Middle English *entertenen*, from Middle French *entretenir*, from Old French *entretenir*, from *entre* (“among”) + *tenir* (“to hold”), from Latin *inter* + *teneō* (“hold, keep”).

senses.definition: A hermit; a religious recluse, someone who lives alone.

core.definition: A person who lives alone, apart from society, usually for religious reasons; a hermit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say it quickly as 'uh'. Americans rhyme the last syllable with 'light', not 'mite' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it describes a choice of solitude and can suggest holiness or eccentricity depending on the speaker.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this word in conversation. You will meet it in religious history, literature, or writing about monks and mystics. In everyday speech, say 'hermit' or 'someone who lives alone in the woods'. Using 'eremite' in casual talk may sound bookish.

distinctions.note: 'Hermit' is the common everyday word for the same thing. 'Eremite' is more formal and mostly appears in religious or scholarly writing.
A recluse avoids people for personal or psychological reasons and need not be religious, while an eremite withdraws for spiritual purposes.

examples.everyday: My neighbor acts like an eremite since his wife passed, but he waves at me every morning.
examples.professional: In the seminary history seminar, our professor described the early eremite communities in the Egyptian desert.
examples.analytical: The early Christian eremite rejected the city not out of hatred for society but in pursuit of undivided attention to God.

nuance.analogy: An eremite is a hermit with a monastery's worth of history behind the word.
nuance.etymology: From Greek erēmitēs, 'of the desert', from erēmos, 'desert, solitary'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as 'ear' with a long vowel; it is closer to 'air'.
Using 'eremite' in casual speech where 'hermit' sounds more natural.

eremite.etymology: Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin, Late Latin *eremita*, from Ancient Greek *ἐρημίτης*, from *ἐρῆμος* + *ίτης*.

core.definition: The Greek and Latin form of Ezra, used in the titles of 1 and 2 Esdras, books outside the Hebrew Bible.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable: EZ-druhs. The 's' after 'z' is a clear 'd' sound, and the last syllable is a reduced 'duhs', not 'dras' as in 'drab'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and scholarly.
nuance.usage_note: Mostly encountered in discussions of the Apocrypha and Septuagint. Numbering is confusing, so scholars specify which edition they mean. Americans typically say 'Ezra' for the canonical book.

distinctions.note: Ezra is the Hebrew form used for the canonical book; Esdras is the Greek and Latin form used for related books.
Nehemiah is a separate figure and book, though in some old numbering it was called 2 Esdras.
Apocrypha is the broader group of books; 1 and 2 Esdras are two of them in the RSV Apocrypha.

examples.everyday: My Bible includes the Apocrypha, so I noticed there's a book called 2 Esdras.
examples.professional: In today's seminar, we'll compare the numbering of Esdras in the Greek, Latin and English traditions.
examples.analytical: 2 Esdras blends Jewish apocalyptic reflection on suffering and theodicy with later Christian additions.

nuance.analogy: Like a name spelled differently in another language: Ezra in Hebrew, Esdras in Greek.
nuance.etymology: From Greek Esdras, a form of the Hebrew name Ezra ('help').
common_mistakes: Saying 'ES-dras' with a short 'a' like 'drab'.
Assuming Esdras is the same as the canonical book of Ezra.
Mixing up the numbering across different Bibles.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV Apocrypha includes 1 Esdras (a Greek retelling of the Judean return from exile) and 2 Esdras (an apocalyptic work with visions). The Hebrew Ezra, 'Yahweh helps,' is the scribe in the canonical book of Ezra, who read the law to the people (Ezra 7:6, 10; Nehemiah 8:1-3).

traditions.view: Orthodox Bibles generally include 1 Esdras as part of the canon, while 2 Esdras is usually in an appendix and not treated as fully canonical.
Catholics do not consider 1 or 2 Esdras (Latin 3 and 4 Esdras) canonical; they appear in the Vulgate appendix, and the canonical books are Ezra and Nehemiah.
Protestants do not treat the Esdras books as Scripture. Anglicans may read them as Apocrypha for instruction, but not to establish doctrine; the RSV Apocrypha includes them.

senses.definition: Fair and impartial; unbiased; just.
senses.example: The questioners are not evenhanded in dealing with the candidates.

core.definition: Treating all sides or people fairly and equally, without favoring one over another.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on EE in 'even,' with secondary stress on HAN in 'handed.' Do not say 'ee-ven' with a long second syllable; the middle syllable is a reduced 'uhn.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises fairness and impartiality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use evenhanded to describe judges, referees, journalists, managers, and anyone expected to be neutral. It often appears in phrases like 'an evenhanded approach' or 'evenhanded treatment.' In everyday talk people also say 'fair' or 'fair-minded,' which is more casual.

distinctions.note: Fair is more general and everyday, while evenhanded stresses equal treatment of parties in a dispute.
Impartial is more formal and emphasizes having no stake in the outcome; evenhanded emphasizes how one behaves toward each side.

examples.everyday: My dad is evenhanded when my brother and I argue, so we both trust him to be fair.
examples.professional: The team lead needs an evenhanded approach when deciding which project gets the new budget.
examples.analytical: A genuinely evenhanded account must represent each position in its strongest form before evaluating it.

nuance.analogy: Like a scale that stays level when both sides are weighed equally, an evenhanded person gives each side the same treatment.
nuance.etymology: From even (level, equal) and handed, a compound formed in English.
common_mistakes: Writing it as two words, even handed, in formal writing; the standard spelling is evenhanded.
Stressing the second syllable of even as a long ee sound.

senses.definition: In an exacting manner.

core.definition: In a way that demands great precision, care, or high standards from oneself or others.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, ZAK. Don't add a separate sound for the t; it blends into the ng, so say it as one smooth run of sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative. It describes demanding standards, which can read as admirable or as harsh depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in writing, reviews, and formal description, not in casual speech. In conversation they usually say 'really strict' or 'very demanding' instead. You might hear it in a review of a restaurant, a film, or a manager's style.

distinctions.note: Strictly describes following rules or limits closely; exactingly describes demanding high standards of quality or performance.
Precisely focuses on accuracy of detail; exactingly focuses on how demanding the standards are.

examples.everyday: My sister's wedding planner was exactingly picky about the flower arrangements.
examples.professional: Our QA lead reviews every release exactingly before it goes to production.
examples.analytical: The theologian argues exactingly for a distinction between divine and human agency.

nuance.analogy: Like a jeweler who checks each stone under a loupe, working exactingly means refusing to accept anything less than fine work.
nuance.etymology: From exacting (demanding, from exact) plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using exactingly for everyday speech, where 'strictly' or 'very carefully' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with exactly, which means precisely or agreed.

senses.definition: Synonym of excellence; the quality of being excellent.

core.definition: A formal title of honor for certain high officials, such as ambassadors or governors; also an older word for excellence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, 'EK.' The final syllable is a reduced 'see,' and the middle vowels are weak, so keep them quick and light.

nuance.connotation: Positive and respectful when used as a title; otherwise dated and somewhat formal.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, Excellency is used as a form of address for ambassadors, governors, and some foreign officials, as in 'Your Excellency.' As a general word for excellence, it is archaic and mainly appears in older texts or the Bible. Modern speakers would normally say excellence.

distinctions.note: Excellence is the everyday word for quality; excellency is mainly a title or an archaic form of the same idea.
Honorable is a title for many officials in the US, while Excellency is used for ambassadors and governors in formal address.

examples.everyday: When the ambassador visited our town, we all called him Your Excellency.
examples.professional: The letter was addressed to His Excellency, the consul general.
examples.analytical: Older translations render the Greek term as excellency, though the modern word excellence captures its meaning more clearly.

nuance.analogy: Like a formal name badge that signals rank rather than everyday quality.
nuance.etymology: From Latin excellentia, the same root as excellence, with the title sense developing in the 1500s.
common_mistakes: Using 'excellency' for everyday praise, where 'excellence' is correct.
Using 'Excellency' as a title without the proper 'His' or 'Your' before it.
nuance.biblical_note: The word excellency appears in older English Bibles, such as the King James translation, for Hebrew terms meaning majesty or splendor. The modern RSV generally uses words such as majesty or glory in these places, so the term is best understood as an archaic rendering.

senses.definition: The act of expelling or the state of being expelled.
senses.example: The scandal involved every member of the high school's football team, resulting in a flurry of expulsions, starting with the quarterback.

core.definition: The act of forcing someone to leave a place, group, or school, often as an official punishment.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPUL, the second syllable. The final syllable is a reduced 'shun', not 'shen' or 'shin'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It usually describes a serious, forced removal, often as a penalty.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use expulsion for students kicked out of school, members removed from a club, or people forced out of a country. In schools, 'suspension' is a milder, temporary punishment, while expulsion is permanent. In casual talk, people often say 'kicked out' instead.

distinctions.note: Suspension is temporary removal; expulsion is usually permanent or long-term removal.
Deportation is the removal of a person from a country by legal authority; expulsion is a broader term for forced removal from any place or group.

examples.everyday: My son got into trouble at school, and we were scared it might end in expulsion.
examples.professional: HR will review the policy before any expulsion from the employee resource group is decided.
examples.analytical: The theologian argued that the expulsion from Eden marks the loss of immediate access to God, not the loss of God's care.

nuance.analogy: Expulsion is like being shown the door: you are not just asked to leave, you are removed for good.
nuance.etymology: From Latin expulsio, from expellere, 'to drive out', from ex- 'out' plus pellere 'to drive'.
common_mistakes: Using expulsion as a verb; the verb is expel.
Confusing expulsion with suspension, which is temporary.

expulsion.etymology: From Middle English *expulsioun*, from Old French *expulsion*, from Latin *expulsiō*.

senses.definition: Exceeding the bounds of something; roving; hence, foreign.
Extreme; wild; excessive; unrestrained.
senses.example: extravagant acts, praise, or abuse

senses.definition: Exorbitant.
Profuse in expenditure; prodigal; wasteful.
senses.example: an extravagant man

core.definition: Spending or costing much more than is reasonable; excessive, lavish, or over the top.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on STRAV, and the middle syllables are quick schwa sounds. Don't pronounce the middle 'a' as a long 'ay'.

nuance.connotation: Often negative (wasteful or excessive), but positive for generous or dramatic gestures; context matters.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it for spending, parties, gifts, and claims: 'an extravagant wedding' or 'extravagant promises'. Calling a person extravagant may sound like criticism. Friendlier options are 'lavish', 'generous', or 'over the top'.

distinctions.note: Lavish is more neutral or positive about generous spending; extravagant more often implies excess or waste.
Excessive simply means too much; extravagant adds the idea of costly indulgence or showiness.
Expensive describes price only; extravagant describes spending that goes beyond reason.

examples.everyday: They threw an extravagant birthday party with a live band and fireworks.
examples.professional: The proposal promises extravagant returns, which makes me suspicious of the assumptions behind it.
examples.analytical: The philosopher's extravagant claim that all knowledge is sensory outruns what the evidence can support.

nuance.analogy: Like ordering every appetizer on the menu: impressive, but well beyond what you need.
nuance.etymology: From Latin extravagans, 'wandering outside', from extra 'outside' and vagari 'to wander'.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for expensive when it implies excess.
Calling someone's gentle generosity extravagant; it sounds like criticism.

extravagant.etymology: Middle English *extravagaunt*, from Middle French *extravagant* and its etymon Medieval Latin *extravagans*, present participle of *extravagor* (“to wander beyond”), from Latin *extra* (“beyond”) + *vagor* (“to wander, stray”).

senses.definition: To report immediately any condition likely to cause a failure, rather than attempting to continue.
To fail earlier rather than later, thus minimizing the fallout and allowing for timely redeployment of resources to another business case or business model.
senses.example: fail fast and pivot

core.definition: To detect a problem early and stop or report it immediately, instead of continuing with a flawed approach, so that losses stay small.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'fast', with 'fail' carrying secondary stress. Link the words smoothly, so it sounds like 'fay-lFAST' with the 'l' moving into the next word.

nuance.connotation: Positive in engineering and business culture, where it is praised as a way to learn quickly; it can sound negative if used to mean carelessness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'fail fast' mainly in software development, startups, and product management, often in phrases like 'We should fail fast and iterate'. It is a cultural slogan, so saying it in a meeting signals agile thinking. In a non-tech setting it may sound odd or flippant.

distinctions.note: 'Fail safe' means a system is designed so that a failure leaves it in a safe state, while 'fail fast' means failures are surfaced quickly so they can be fixed.
'Fail forward' emphasizes learning from failure and moving on, while 'fail fast' emphasizes detecting failure early.

examples.everyday: My sister says she wants to fail fast on the new recipe, so she's trying a small batch first.
examples.professional: Let's fail fast on this prototype and test the checkout flow with real users this week.
examples.analytical: The design philosophy of 'fail fast' assumes that early, visible errors are cheaper than hidden ones discovered in production.

nuance.analogy: Fail fast is like a smoke alarm: it goes off early and loudly, so you can respond before the whole house burns down.
nuance.etymology: A modern software and business phrase; its origin is not precisely recorded.
common_mistakes: Stressing 'fail' instead of 'fast' so that it sounds like 'FAIL fast' in an unnatural way.
Using it as a noun phrase, as in 'a fail fast'; it is normally a verb phrase or adjective 'fail-fast'.
